Pexels · 18312070
Choosing with care
A good way to buy what we need combines practical structure with an awareness of other people. Neither a rigid plan nor complete
improvisation is sufficient on its own; both need to be judged in context.
The practical case is straightforward: a short shopping list helps us buy only what we can use. Consider how we check the kitchen
before choosing fruit and vegetables. The benefit is not merely efficiency. A modest arrangement prevents avoidable confusion,
leaving attention available for the activity itself rather than for problems that could have been anticipated.
Consideration adds a second, equally important dimension: asking questions helps us compare choices fairly. In this situation, we
ask how long the bread will keep before deciding how much to buy. A decision can be convenient for one person while creating
difficulty for another, so its value depends partly on whose needs it recognises.
The most useful approach therefore brings structure and consideration together. Preparation establishes a workable starting point;
attention to other people keeps it responsive. Success should be assessed by how well the arrangement serves the experience,
rather than by how closely events follow the original plan.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a focused main idea. Develop one supporting reason in each body paragraph, with a concrete example.
Conclude by connecting the two reasons without introducing a new argument. Use the structure as a model; write about an
experience of your own.
Compare your first answer with this question: What two reasons support the main idea? Explain one example. (Model: The two
reasons are that a short shopping list helps us buy only what we can use and that asking questions helps us compare choices fairly.
One example is that we check the kitchen before choosing fruit and vegetables.)
